title: Single-Head Attention in High Dimensions: A Theory of Generalization, Weights Spectra, and Scaling Laws
claim: Exact theory predicts both test-error curves and evolving weight spectra, matching simulations across sample regimes and revealing spectral splitting at large data.
layout: 2 regions: left line plot, right 2x2 spectrum histograms; dashed lines link alphas
description: The figure has two parts. On the left is a line plot of test error against the sample ratio α=n/d² on a log axis. A solid blue theory curve falls from about 0.43 and plateaus near 0.08. Black crosses (GD, κ=1) and magenta dots with error bars (GD, κ=0.75) lie on the curve. Four vertical grey dashed lines mark α values 0.1, 0.5, 4 and 40. On the right is a 2×2 grid of singular-value histograms, one per marked α. Grey bars show simulations, a blue theory curve overlays them, and a red dashed curve shows the target spectrum. A tall spike sits at zero. At large α a separate low-value bulk appears next to the main bulk.
caption: (Left) Test error of the ERM estimator Eq. (3) (Claim 3.1, Eq. (13)) compared with Adam simulations at d = 100 (64 instances, error bars = standard deviation) as a function of the number of samples α = n/d2, where we use κ = 0.75, 1 (model width) and parameters λ = 0.01, ∆= 0.5, T = 2, β = β0 = 1 for the MP target (Section 3, κ0 = 0.5). Theory and simulations agree. (Right) Singular value spectrum of the trained weights from theory (blue, Claim 4.1, Eq. (21)) vs. Adam simulations (grey histograms) at α = 0.05, 0.5, 4, 40 (d = 200, 64 runs, 2000 samples in the test set). The asymptotic spectrum of the target is shown in red dashed. The theory also captures the delta peak at zero. For large α, the spectrum splits into two bulks.
abstract: Trained attention layers exhibit striking and reproducible spectral structure of the weights, including low-rank collapse, bulk deformation, and isolated spectral outliers, yet the origin of these phenomena and their implications for generalization remain poorly understood. We study empirical risk minimization in a single-head tied-attention layer trained on synthetic high-dimensional sequence tasks generated from the attention-indexed model. Using tools from random matrix theory, spin-glass theory, and approximate message passing, we obtain an exact high-dimensional characterization of training and test error, interpolation and recovery thresholds, and the spectrum of the key and query matrices. Our theory predicts the full singular-value distribution of the trained query-key map, including low-rank structure and isolated spectral outliers, in qualitative agreement with observations in more realistic transformers. Finally, for targets with power-law spectra, we show that learning proceeds through sequential spectral recovery, leading to the emergence of power-law scaling laws.
